title: The quick guide to fall vaccines and when you should get them
gist: Despite RFK Jr.'s disbanding of a legally-invalidated CDC vaccine advisory panel, this fall's flu, COVID-19, and RSV vaccine rollout is proceeding largely as normal in the US, with major insurers continuing free coverage through 2027, medical societies stepping in with their own evidence-based recommendations, and a new higher-efficacy mRNA flu vaccine (Moderna's mFlusiva) facing coverage uncertainty due to its late approval and lack of prior CDC panel recommendation.

insights.claim: The CDC's vaccine advisory committee is nonfunctioning after a federal judge ruled in March that RFK Jr.'s appointees to the panel were illegally installed, voiding their prior policy changes, leaving the US without an official federal body setting vaccine recommendations for the 2026-27 season.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A structurally absent federal vaccine advisory function means insurance coverage and provider guidance now depend on ad hoc medical-society consensus rather than statutory process, a fragility worth monitoring into next flu/COVID season.
insights.locator: A federal judge ruled in March

insights.claim: A coalition of major medical organizations (American Medical Association, Vaccine Integrity Project, AAP, AAFP, ACOG, IDSA) has stepped in to produce its own evidence-based respiratory virus immunization recommendations for 2026-27, filling the void left by the non-functioning CDC panel — a repeat of what happened last year.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Medical societies effectively substituting for a dysfunctional federal advisory process for a second consecutive year signals this may become a durable institutional workaround rather than a one-off gap.
insights.locator: leading medical organizations have stepped in to fill the void

insights.claim: Major insurance plans have agreed to continue covering CDC-panel-previously-recommended vaccines, including seasonal flu/COVID/RSV shots, at no charge through at least the end of 2027, independent of the advisory committee's current dysfunction.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Locks in consumer-facing vaccine access/affordability for over a year regardless of ongoing federal advisory-panel turmoil, reducing near-term downside risk to vaccination rates from the policy chaos.
insights.locator: Major insurance plans have agreed to continue covering vaccines

insights.claim: Moderna's mRNA flu vaccine mFlusiva, approved for adults 50 and up in early August 2026, was found 27 percent more effective than a standard flu shot in trials but may cause more mild side effects like fatigue and injection-site soreness.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A meaningfully higher-efficacy mRNA flu vaccine reaching market is a notable clinical and commercial milestone for Moderna's respiratory franchise, contingent on resolving the coverage uncertainty below.
insights.locator: The biggest uncertainty this season will likely be with the new mRNA flu vaccine

insights.claim: mFlusiva's coverage is uncertain because it lacks a prior recommendation from the CDC's advisory committee: Medicare is expected to cover it and some state Medicaid programs may as well, but other federal programs like Vaccines for Adults may not, and commercial insurance coverage is unclear.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The CDC advisory-panel dysfunction has a direct, concrete commercial consequence: it creates real reimbursement uncertainty for Moderna's newest, highest-margin flu product right at launch, a factor relevant to near-term Moderna respiratory revenue.
insights.locator: It’s unclear how available this vaccine will be this year

insights.claim: Despite the policy chaos, COVID-19 vaccine access for people under 65 remains largely unchanged from last year: major pharmacy chains like CVS and Walgreens continue to let most people self-attest a qualifying reason without a prescription, with a few state exceptions such as Louisiana requiring a prescription.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Real-world consumer access has proven more resilient to federal advisory dysfunction than the regulatory headlines suggest, useful context for assessing actual vaccination-rate risk this season.
insights.locator: Big pharmacies, like CVS and Walgreens

insights.claim: The optimal flu shot timing window is late September through end of October, since protection takes about two weeks to develop and wanes over the season, which typically peaks December-February and can stretch to May.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A concrete consumer-actionable timing rule for optimizing vaccine efficacy against the flu season's typical peak.
insights.locator: The best time to get a flu vaccine is generally the span

insights.claim: The RSV vaccination window for pregnant people has been updated this year: the recommended period expanded from September 1-January 31 last year to September 1-March 1, reflecting new data on RSV transmission trends.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A concrete evidence-based update showing the non-CDC medical-society recommendation process is still incorporating new epidemiological data, not just carrying forward stale guidance.
insights.locator: This recommendation includes a notable update
